newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Gonzalez begs for calm in "dirty war" row.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Gonzalez begs for calm in "dirty war" row.

text.p: Former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez pleaded for calm on Thursday after the new Spanish government's number two, who has blamed him for a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque rebels, was himself called as a court witness.
"We should maintain a great serenity in the face of certain types of behaviour," Gonzalez told journalists, referring to comments made by Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos.

Earlier, lawyers defending an anti-terrorist police chief in the dirty war investigation announced they wanted Alvarez Cascos to testify because he had directly blamed Gonzalez for the 1983-87 campaign of kidnaps, torture and murder against ETA separatist rebels.

"We filed a petition to hear the testimony of Alvarez Cascos based on his statements relating to Gonzalez and the GAL," one of the lawyers told Reuters. GAL is the Spanish acronym for Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups, the shadowy front for the death squads that waged the illegal campaign.
Alvarez Cascos is in charge of Spain's secret services and has unrivalled access to top-secret information. He set off a political storm last weekend when he accused Gonzalez of organising the GAL.

Gonzalez, who said last week there was no state terrorism during his 13-year rule, has always denied any knowledge of the activities of the death squads that killed nearly 30 people -- one third of them by mistake.

The deputy prime minister said at the weekend that there had not been "state terrorism" but "bodeguilla terrorism", alluding to the wine bar in the prime minister's residence where Gonzalez had entertained close friends.
His comment sparked fierce reaction from other Socialists who demanded he resign and from members of the left-wing United Left coalition who said he should testify.

Juan Carlos Rodriguez Ibarra, Socialist leader of the Extremadura region, said his party should break off relations with the ruling Popular Party (PP) until Alvarez Cascos had shown he had proof against Gonzalez or until he was sacked.

"It (the comment about Gonzalez) wasn't a spontaneous action, but premeditated with the goal of regaining the PP's loss of voter confidence just a few months after coming to power," he wrote in a letter to newspaper El Mundo.

The Catalan coalition -- current PP allies and former allies of the Socialists -- criticised the disintegrating relations among the political parties and warned that they could plunge the country back into the crisis that led to the last general election.

"We hope there is no return to the climate of the past few years in Spanish politics," Catalan leader Jordi Pujol said on Wednesday, urging the conservatives and socialists to avoid "poking about in the wounds of the dirty war".
But the conservatives, who initially dismissed Alvarez Cascos' statement as personal opinion, appeared on Thursday to embrace it as a government position.

The Supreme Court justice investigating the GAL case must now decide whether or not to study the petition before it becomes clear whether Alvarez Cascos will actually be summoned, the lawyer said. There is no set timetable for the rulings.
A lawyer representing the GAL victims and their families joined the petition, saying it was "vital" that Alvarez Cascos testify in the dirty war investigation.

"If he made these statements it would be because he has proof that Felipe Gonzalez and those near him in the government or in his circle could have participated in the activities of the GAL," attorney Teodoro Mota said.
